extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about which type of Brahmin is worthy of receiving alms: those who wear caste marks or those who do not.

attributes.topic: Criteria for worthy recipients of alms

extraction_text: Bhishma responds that Brahmins who diligently perform their caste duties, whether they wear caste marks or not, are worthy of receiving alms because both types are pious.

attributes.key_point: Worthiness based on duty performance, not outward marks

extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks about the fault in giving offerings meant for gods and ancestors to a twice-born person with devotion.
Bhishma explains that even a person with a harsh nature becomes pure through devotion, and their actions become pure in all circumstances.
Yudhishthira asks about the contradiction regarding examining Brahmins for god-worship rituals versus ancestor-worship rituals.
Bhishma explains that in god-worship rituals, merit comes directly from the gods, not from the officiating Brahmin, and gods bestow favors upon worshippers through rituals.
Bhishma adds that Brahmins should always be teachers of Vedic truth, citing the wise sage Markandeya.
Yudhishthira asks which of five types of people should receive alms: strangers, learned people, relatives by marriage, ascetics, or those who perform regular sacrifices.

Bhishma responds that the first three types (strangers, learned people, relatives by marriage) are qualified if they are pure in birth, diligent in duties, learned, good-hearted, humble, honest, and truthful.
Bhishma cites the views of four beings: Earth Goddess, Sage Kashyapa, Fire God, and Markandeya.
Earth Goddess says that just as a lump of clay dissolves in the ocean, any sin dissolves in the three actions of a person.
Kashyapa says that knowledge of Vedas, Vedangas, Samkhya philosophy, Puranas, and good birth cannot absolve a person of misconduct.
Fire God says that a Brahmin who studies scriptures, thinks highly of himself, and uses his knowledge to ruin others' reputations commits the sin of betraying truth and loses access to happy worlds.
Markandeya says that if one weighs a thousand horse sacrifices against truth on a scale, the former might not reach half the weight of the latter.
Bhishma concludes that these four—Earth Goddess, Kashyapa, Agni, and the descendant of Bhrigu (Markandeya)—are beings of infinite energy.
坚战 (Yudhishthira) asks 毗湿摩 (Bhishma) whether a Brahmin who has taken a vow of celibacy gains merit by eating food offered to ancestors by others.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) responds that such a Brahmin who has studied all Vedas and is in the Brahmacharya stage violates his vows by eating that food.
坚战 (Yudhishthira) asks about the definitive statement on Dharma, noting that wise sages have said Dharma has multiple purposes and paths.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) defines the marks of morality as non-injury to life, truthfulness, avoidance of anger, kindness, self-control, and uprightness.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) warns about hypocrites who preach morality but don't practice it, and those who give donations to such people will fall into hell for ten years, eating filth.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) states that those who refuse to give ancestral offerings to Brahmins observing Brahmacharya will suffer in a world full of misery.
坚战 (Yudhishthira) asks what is higher than Brahmacharya, what is the highest mark of Dharma, and what is the mark of purity.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) answers that abstaining from honey and meat is higher than Brahmacharya, following rules is Dharma, and tranquility is the mark of purity.
坚战 (Yudhishthira) asks when to practice Dharma, when to pursue material gain, and when to enjoy happiness.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) advises to accumulate wealth in youth, then practice Dharma, then pursue enjoyment, but not to be excessively attached to any one.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) teaches to respect Brahmins, serve teachers, be kind to all beings, be gentle in conduct, and speak pleasantly.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) equates lying in court, slandering others before the king, and mistreating teachers with Brahminicide.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) equates harming the king's body and striking a cow with fetal murder.
毗湿摩 (Bhishma) equates neglecting sacrificial fire, abandoning Vedic study, and shouting at Brahmins with Brahminicide.
坚战 (Yudhishthira) asks what kind of Brahmin is noble and worthy of respect, what kind gives the best results when given donations, and what kind should be given food.
Bhishma describes the qualities of a worthy Brahmin who deserves donations.

attributes.action: Bhishma explains that a Brahmin who is free from anger, performs duties according to dharma, always adheres to truth, and does not find self-restraint painful is noble and worthy of respect. Donating to such a Brahmin yields excellent results.

extraction_text: Bhishma lists additional virtues that make a Brahmin deserving of donations.

attributes.action: He states that a Brahmin who abandons pride, tolerates everything, has clear goals, controls senses, works for the welfare of all beings, is compassionate, and possesses these qualities is worthy of donations, which bring excellent results.

extraction_text: Bhishma continues describing the ideal qualities of a Brahmin.

attributes.action: He says a Brahmin who can suppress greed, maintain purity of body and mind, is learned, has a sense of shame, speaks truthfully, and diligently performs duties is worthy of donations, which yield excellent results.

extraction_text: Bhishma explains the qualifications based on Vedic knowledge and duties.

attributes.action: He mentions that a Brahmin who studies all four Vedas and their branches while actively performing six duties is considered by ancient sages as qualified to receive donations.

extraction_text: Bhishma emphasizes the benefits of donating to a qualified Brahmin.

attributes.action: He states that donating to a Brahmin with the above qualities yields excellent results, and donating to one with genuinely good qualities multiplies one's merit a thousandfold.

extraction_text: Bhishma highlights the power of a learned and dutiful Brahmin.

attributes.action: He explains that a Brahmin with exceptional wisdom, mastery of Vedic knowledge, and strict adherence to scriptural duties can alone save an entire family.

extraction_text: Bhishma advises on the types of donations and their benefits.

attributes.action: He says that donating cows, horses, wealth, food, or other items to such a Brahmin can prevent suffering in the next life, and an excellent twice-born can single-handedly save a family.

extraction_text: Bhishma concludes with the importance of selecting a qualified recipient.

attributes.action: He stresses that choosing a qualified recipient is crucial. One should travel far to invite a Brahmin known for excellent qualities and revered by the virtuous, and honor him appropriately in every possible way.

extraction_text: The text notes the end of the chapter.

attributes.action: This concludes Chapter 23 of the Shanti Parva (Book of Instructions) in the Mahabharata.
